evidence: Diom. p. 350 P.; Prisc. p. 808 P. (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A term of the later grammarians; Servius calls it gerundīvus modus. A verbal noun with only the oblique cases: legendī librōs causā, for the sake of reading books (Traupman 234); it has no nominative, gerundium eget cāsū nōminātīvō (241).

phrases.latin: Gerundium quid est? — Est nōmen verbāle.
phrases.english: What is a gerund? — It is a verbal noun.

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency (printed page numbers): p. 234, p. 241, p. 246.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
